Uniform Title: Parāprāveśikā Author: Kṣemarāja Description: E-text transcribed from Volume 15 of the Kashmir Series of Texts and Studies.

Notes: E-text transcribed by the staff of Muktabodha under the supervision of Mark S.G. Dyczkowski. Revision 0: 11/28/2005. Publisher: Research Department, Jammu and Kashmir State. Publication year: 1918.
Place of publication: Bombay;
Country of publication: India; Bombay, 1918.
Oṃ, salutations to Śiva, the self of all principles;
now follows the introduction to the Supreme.

We praise the consciousness that is the heart of the Supreme Lord— consisting of the universe and transcending it— which manifests in the form of the powers beginning with Parā, composed by the illustrious and eminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Kṣemarāja.
In this context, the Supreme Lord is indeed of the nature of light; and as for this light— surely,
even though the Supreme Lord has light as His essential nature, does He possess a nature of pure consciousness alone, like the proponents of the quiescent Brahman?
Anticipating this objection, he says, "And light" (*prakāśaśca*). [Light] has the nature of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*).

Reflective awareness is twofold, by virtue of being either limited or unlimited. Among these, in the case of limitation, there would be a delimitation of the light of consciousness by that [reflective awareness] appropriate to subjects such as the void (*śūnya*), and so forth.

With the intention that this may be so, he says: "What is called reflective awareness (*vimarśa*). And that reflective awareness consists in the wonder of full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhantā*) during emission (*sṛṣṭi*) in the form of the universe, during persistence (*sthiti*) through its manifestation, and during withdrawal (*saṃhāra*) through the act of assimilating [the universe] into one's own self; such is the meaning. "What is called" (*nāma*).

The spontaneous flash of the thought "I am" occurs by way of manifesting the universe, illuminating the universe, and withdrawing the universe. If— [that is to say,] if the light of the sun and so forth were devoid of self-reflection (*vimarśa*), it would, due to its dependence on another, fall into the category of the insentient (*jaḍa*).

The sense is that if one were to resort to a lack of autonomy, then by that very lack of self-reflective awareness (*nirvimarśatā*), even the light of consciousness (*saṃvitprakāśa*) would result in a state of non-existence. [If it were] without self-reflective awareness, it would follow that it is powerless and insentient. And this very self-reflective awareness is: consciousness (*cit*), sentience (*caitanya*), the supreme speech (*aparāvāk*) arising from its own inherent essence.
In the scriptures, it is proclaimed by such terms as "sovereignty," "the primary lordship of the Supreme Self," "agency," "vibration" (sphurattā), "essence," "heart," and "throb" (spanda).
In this system of the Śaiva teachings, the predominance of reflective awareness (vimarśa) belongs precisely to the light of consciousness (saṃvitprakāśa).

That which is proclaimed in various scriptures is indeed handed down through the diverse linguistic expressions of those respective traditions; for instance, with the intention that "consciousness" (*caitanya*)—
which is nothing other than reflective awareness (*vimarśa*)— is the primary nature of the Self, [the scripture] uses a term denoting a property (*dharma*).

The indication has been made by means of a word. Likewise, regarding "the supreme speech (aparāvāk) arisen from its own essence": it is called *vāk* because it speaks—that is, it expresses the universe through reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*). That very [speech] is "supreme" (*parā*) because it is the substratum of all other forms of reflective awareness and because of its fullness; for this very reason...

Because its expansion is unceasing, and because it is ever-arisen as the perfectly full body of consciousness in the form of "I," it is said to be "arisen by its own inherent nature" (*svarasodita*). Likewise, it is "sovereignty" (*svātantrya*); and sovereignty consists in the joining and separating [of objects], whereby the state of "this-ness" (*idantā*) is projected outwards from itself.
It joins [the self] with its own nature, and having joined it, it also disjoins it;

and on the stages such as emptiness (*śūnya*), it causes it to become subservient—it is thus, by such characteristics, that it establishes a distinction from the insentient. Likewise, there is sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).

Regarding "independence from anything else at the beginning of the universal creation": this means that he is not subject to the constraints of necessity (*niyati*) by being under the sway of another's will, as is the case with Brahmā and others who occupy the office of the *māyā*-womb.
Likewise, regarding "agency" (*kartṛtva*): this very agency consists in [acting] through the supramundane...

The manifestation of the entire universe—from Śiva down to the earth—which exists as a unity within one's own internal light through the relationship of cause and effect, occurs by way of the "this-ness" (idantā) [of the object], like a creation of a yogi.
Thus, "vibration" (sphurattā) refers to the connection with vibration; this does not exist for things such as a jar, for if it did—
Otherwise, either everything such as jars and the like would manifest to everyone at all times, or nothing would manifest to anyone;

thus, the consequence of universal omniscience or its opposite would follow. Therefore, the meaning is that by saying "it manifests to me," one's own manifestation (*sphuraṇa*) is indicated. "Essence" (*sāra*) means a non-trivial form; that...

It is precisely the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) of the Supreme Lord. It is called the "Heart" (*hṛdaya*) because it is the locus where the universe is established. It is called "Vibration" (*spanda*) because it is the manifestation of movement within the unmoving light of consciousness, which, although not distinct from that [consciousness], appears as if it were distinct.
The meaning is "the illumination of the universe. Therefore,

demonstrating that it is precisely through the majesty of the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) that the Supreme Lord shines forth by His own self in the form of the manifestation of the manifold variety of the universe—
He concludes the definition of the power of reflective awareness (*vimarśa-śakti*) with the words "for this very reason.

The underlying sense is that since alternative causes such as *māyā* or *prakṛti* are undermined by the dilemmas of being either different or non-different [from the effect], their status as the creator of the world is not tenable.
The uncreated "I"— the Supreme Lord, whose true nature is self-luminous—

manifests and shines forth through His supreme power (*pārameśvarī śakti*) as the world extending from Śiva down to the earth. This alone is what constitutes the manifestation of the Supreme Lord in the form of the universe.
"This alone is the ultimate agency; by its very manifestation, even the universe, while being made manifest, attains the state of non-inertness"—thus he says, "This alone.
[The agency and non-inertness of this world—[but indeed, what is the nature of that which has the world as its object?]

Is its state of being an effect [related to the Supreme Lord] through difference or non-difference? If there were difference, the so-called sovereignty (*svātantrya*) of the Supreme Lord, who is its creator, would be undermined; if there were non-difference, how could that [sovereignty] exist? Anticipating this doubt, he says "of the world" (*jagataḥ*). This is because this world cannot be cognized without the supreme light [of consciousness].

The attainment of its own self-nature is difficult to accomplish; because it relies upon and takes as its support that [Self], it comes to possess a body consisting of its manifestation—this alone is its state of being an effect.
It is only through the sovereignty of Māyā that, despite its non-difference, there is a conventional treatment of it as if it were different due to the appearance of duality.

This is the intended meaning. Even "being an effect" consists precisely in having its manifestation dependent upon this [consciousness]. Thus, the world, being of such a nature, is non-different from the Great Lord, the agent whose very form is light.
For if it were a different object of cognition, it would not manifest; whereas, in the state of non-difference, the universe shines forth.

[He would] be bold [to claim otherwise], for otherwise, due to the voidness of its own nature, the worldly transaction consisting of rejection, acquisition, and so forth, would perish; with this intention, he says: "if there were a separate object of cognition" (bhinnavedyatve).
Because manifestation would be impossible, nothing at all would exist. By this [he means]: "Now, if the world..."

To ward off the doubt that— since the world, whose sole nature is light, appears as non-different from the Supreme Lord, a distinction of identity (sārūpyabheda) within the Supreme Lord would be unavoidable, and by that [distinction] He too might become concealed— he says: "By this."

On the contrary, even though it has been attained within one's own self, it would perish by itself due to the obscuration of its light; this is the meaning. Furthermore, the luminous form of this Blessed Lord is never concealed from the world, having attained stability through this very manifestation.
How could this manifest world, which is the very life-breath of the Self, be obstructed? And how could the Self remain established by itself after having obstructed it?
Therefore, its instrumental factors, such as the knower and so forth, must operate upon a pre-established Lord.

Taking the intention that [objects] cannot [be established by themselves], [the author] says "and therefore of this" (*ataścāsya*) with respect to the object: since even the cognizer who performs the injunctions and so forth exists in that same nature [as the object], its establishment does not depend upon a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*);
therefore, its self-luminosity is established by experience.
Its existence consists in its being of the nature of a cognizing subject (pramātṛ) who effects the synthesis of "this is a proof" and "this is a refutation," or "this is a means of valid cognition.
To this [question]— what is the proof for its existence?— [it is replied:]...
Even if one were to grant the existence of such an entity, what proof is there for its having such a nature?
Thus, by way of posing this question, the self-luminosity of Maheśvara—who is established as prior [to all]—is proven by the self-awareness of everyone. Furthermore:

[He says "Moreover" (kiṃ ca) to express that] since the light of consciousness alone, which constitutes the very life of all, postulates the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) within the illusory worldly transaction (*māyīyavyavahāra*), no means of knowledge whatsoever is required there because it is already established beforehand. Furthermore, everything else, in relation to the supreme light, is insentient (*jaḍa*).

[The meaning is: how could that which is incapable of even illuminating itself endeavor to establish another? [Furthermore,] regarding that very means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) by depending upon which a [particular] means of valid cognition becomes valid...

Furthermore, what utility is there for this wretched means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), which consists merely in the illumination of a novel object, when the Knower— who is of a single nature as the illuminator, who is eternally manifest, who transcends all objects of cognition such as the body, vital breath, and the experience of pleasure and pain dependent upon Him, and who is the source of all valid cognitions— is already established? What [utility is there]?

Regarding "application" (*upayoga*): that which is called a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) becomes a means of knowledge by producing a repose characterized as valid cognition within the subject (*pramātṛ*), in the form of a novel manifestation;
and the subject, because it is eternally manifest, possesses an uninterrupted manifestation and [integrates] all cognitions within its own self.
Since it partakes of an inward-turned form, how could a novel manifestation be of use therein, and where else could its cognition find its final rest? Therefore,
the application of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) pertains only to objects of cognition such as the body, the vital breath, blue, pleasure, and so forth, but not [to that inward-turned nature].
In the Supreme Lord, who constitutes the very life of the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), it has been said:
"Even those means of valid cognition which extend life to objects—
their supreme life-force is that very same Supreme Lord."
Thus, because its essence consists of the reflective awareness of the full *ahantā* (I-consciousness) composed of the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*)—
where "composed of the mass of sounds" means that which consists of the collection of phonemes beginning with *a* and ending with *ha*, which internalizes the entire universe— [it is so called].

That reflective awareness of full subjectivity (*pūrṇāhantā-parāmarśa*), whose nature is the repose in self-sovereignty that does not look toward any other face, and which takes the form "I alone, whose essence is light, am manifest"— that very [awareness] is the essence, the non-trivial form, of that [reality].
The meaning is that "existence" (*bhāva*) arises from that cause. Supreme Śiva alone is the manifold universe (*prapañca*) consisting of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*).
Regarding the thirty-six principles: "the state of being those [principles] is the principle" (*tattvam*); thus, among the various classes [of categories],...
That which appears as one and undivided, serving as the basis for classification, is the *tattva* (principle);

for example, mountains, trees, cities, and so forth, as well as rivers, lakes, oceans, and so forth, share the nature of earth and the nature of water. Furthermore: 1. Śiva, 2. Śakti, 3. Sadāśiva, 4. [Īśvara].

Īśvara (5), Śuddhavidyā (6), Māyā (7), Kalā (8), Vidyā (9), Rāga (10), Kāla (11), Niyati (12), Puruṣa (13), Prakṛti (14), Buddhi (15), Ahaṃkāra (16), Manas (17), Śrotra (18), Tvak (19), Cakṣus (20), Jihvā (21), Ghrāṇa (22), Vāk (23), Pāṇi (24), Pāda (25).
The anus (26), the generative organ (27), sound (28), touch (29), form (30), taste (31), smell (32), ether (33), air (34), fire (35), water (36), and earth—these are they.
Now, their characteristics: therein, that which is called the Śiva-tattva consists of will, knowledge, and...
Paramaśiva is of the nature of the essence of absolute, full bliss consisting of action;
he is the state transcending all categories (*tattva*), consisting of the wonder of the full "I-consciousness" (*pūrṇāhaṃtā*) flashing forth within all subjects.

The Śiva-principle is the embodiment of great light, capable of receiving the reflections of hundreds of thousands of cycles of creation and withdrawal contained within the entire mass of principles. Precisely this is the principle of the power of will (*icchā-śakti-tattva*), which is the very first vibration of the Supreme Lord when He has assumed the desire to create this world.
[By the very majesty of His own sovereignty, through the desire to manifest externally and the intensification of the wonder of supreme bliss, the reflective awareness "I" is the *śakti-tattva*. (p.
7) Because His will is unimpeded, this world, though already existent, begins to sprout forth.
The Sadāśiva-tattva is that form which exists veiled by the "I-ness" (ahaṃtā) of its own self;
[when the Supreme Lord, while remaining in the substratum of pure consciousness alone, causes the "this-portion" (idamaṃśa) to manifest within the "I-portion" (ahamaṃśa), then for Him...]

The Sadāśiva-tattva has desire as its primary characteristic because it is indistinct, owing to its having as its object a mass of phenomena that are like paintings on a mind that has just been opened. The Īśvara-tattva exists enveloping the sprouted universe within the "I-sense" (ahaṃtā). And when the "this" aspect (idamaṃśa) has become manifest, [it is the "I" aspect...]
At that time, he sprinkles [the self] with the *Īśvara-tattva*, which is primarily characterized by the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*).

Although there is no difference between the two aforementioned *tattvas* regarding the reflective awareness of "I" (*ahaṃ-vimarśa*), there is a distinction based on whether the "this" aspect (*idam-aṃśa*) is turbid or non-turbid.

The realization of the identity between "I" and "this" is *śuddhavidyā*; furthermore, when the manifestation of the objective aspect (*idamaṃśa*), which resides within the mass of entities characterized by fully developed duality,
shines forth as being inherent in pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), the subjective aspect (*ahamaṃśa*) emerges, as is the case for those who advocate non-dualism-in-difference (*bhedādvaitavādins*).
The reflective awareness of the Lord as "I am this," according to the analogy of the evenly balanced scales,
is the *vidyā-tattva*, which is characterized primarily by the power of action (*kriyā-śakti*). The manifestation of duality within entities that are one's own essential nature is *māyā*.

Taking the form of non-obstruction in the accomplishment of even the most difficult of tasks, it causes a firmly rooted conceit of subjectivity (*pramātṛtā*) regarding that which is insentient and empty; manifesting even entities consisting solely of consciousness as if they were distinct, it conceals its own true nature.
And Māyā is the material cause of all entities beginning from Kalā and ending with the Earth;
however, when the Supreme Lord, by means of His supreme power of Māyā—which is synonymous with absolute freedom (*svātantrya*)—[manifests] His own nature... (p. 8)
When it assumes the state of a contracted grasper, it is then designated as the "Person" (puruṣa).
This very one, deluded by *māyā* and bound by *karman*—[meaning, conceiving of actions as the binders of its own self]—is the transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*). [Regarding the term *saṃsārī*:]
Because it wanders [through births], it is called a "wanderer" (saṃsārī). Even the body, by maintaining a similarity of form across childhood, youth, and so forth, appears as if it were wandering;
however, the wandering of the intellect and other faculties persists even in another birth. Although he is non-different from the Supreme Lord, this [individual] possesses delusion.

It would not belong to the Supreme Lord— unlike a magician who produces illusions at will; for He possesses sovereignty manifested through knowledge (*vidyā*), that is, through the power of manifesting His own essential nature.

He has attained the state of higher knowledge (*abhijñā*) and sovereignty; for this very reason, he is "consisting of consciousness" (*ciddhana*), meaning that even his body and so forth are nothing but pure awareness, devoid of any admixture with the insentient nature of the universe. He is liberated as one whose essence is consciousness (*ciddhana*). [The term "liberated" means...]

The sense is that because of the cessation of the bond of rebirth, he is fit to be designated as "liberated" even while the body remains; however, when the body has fallen, he is indeed the very nature of Paramaśiva. He is Paramaśiva himself.
His [attributes] are universal agency, omniscience, fullness, eternity, and pervasiveness.
Although the powers (*śakti*) are undifferentiated, by assuming limitation they become the forms of *kalā*, *vidyā*, *rāga*, *kāla*,
and *niyati*; just as for one whose entire property has been confiscated by a king, out of compassion a small amount is given for the sake of survival.

Wealth is given; likewise, to consciousness that has attained a state of atomicity (*aṇutva*)—from which omniscience and other qualities have been removed—something is bestowed in its place: the ultimate reality of limited agency (*kiṃcitkartṛtā*) and so forth, namely *kalā* and the rest.
This is the intended meaning. Thus they arise. Here, regarding the name *kalā*: [the term *kalā*...]
That by which this person is unable to do everything and instead performs only certain things, such as a jar, is *vidyā* (knowledge); it is the cause of his limited agency,
for by means of it he knows only certain objects present before him, such as a jar, but not an object that is distant or concealed.

The cause of limited knowledge is passion (*rāga*), which is an attachment to sense objects characterized by the thought, "This is useful to me; may I have more of it; may I never cease to exist. For time indeed governs all phenomena.

The sequence is the delimiting factor for those things whose nature consists of manifestation and non-manifestation; [as it is said: "the sequence is the delimiting factor" means that by conceptualizing entities likewise through the nature of knowledge and action—as "I have known, I know, I shall know," and "I have done, I do, I shall do"—it delimits them.]
The source of the elements (bhūtādi), necessity (niyati)—[regarding "necessity" as follows]: "This must be done by me;

this, such as the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha) which has heaven and so forth as its fruit, is precisely what must be performed by me, and not [acts] like the killing of a Brahmin which has hell and so forth as its fruit. And furthermore, from necessity alone...
The nature of necessity (*niyati*) consists of many forms, such as the idea that "the effect is necessarily determined by its cause.
It is the cause of restriction, such that one thinks, "This must be done by me; this must not be done.
Because these five [categories] conceal his true nature, they are called "coverings" (*kañcuka*).

The meaning is that, although it is distinct from its own essential nature (*svarūpa*), it remains as if non-distinct, veiling the nature of perfect consciousness (*pūrṇasaṃvit*). It is said that *prakṛti* is the root cause of the principles (*tattva*) beginning with the Great One (*mahat*) and ending with earth; and this—
The state of equilibrium of sattva, rajas, and tamas— which consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion, and whose natures are illumination, activity, and restraint— is the "common" (sāmānya).
Form (*rūpa*) means that state wherein no relationship of part and whole (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) is perceived.

It is a state of equilibrium (*sāmyāvasthā*), undifferentiated in form, and determinative (*niścayakāriṇī*). [Regarding "determinative": it refers to a determination of the form "this is such-and-such."]

The intellect (*buddhi*) is that which holds the reflection of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-pratibimba-dhāriṇī*)— the sense being that, because it is preeminent in its sattva-quality and possesses clarity, it is capable of receiving reflections. That which is called the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) is the notion "this is mine."
The means for the conceit "this is mine" is the intellect (buddhi); the means for volition (saṃkalpa) is the mind (manas).

These three constitute the internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa), so called because they are the instruments for grasping internal objects such as pleasure and the like. Their function consists of the qualities (guṇas) acting in a relationship of principal and subordinate.
It is the cause of the group of effects to be described, such as the elements and the sense organs;
and it consists of the five [organs]— the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose— which are the means for the sequential apprehension of objects consisting of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell.

The organs of knowledge (jñānendriyāṇi). The five organs of action (karmendriyāṇi), which are the means for the activities consisting of speaking, grasping, moving, excreting, and procreation, are, in their respective order: speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals. Sound, touch, form, taste, [smell]...
Odors are the five general forms; these are the *tanmātras*. [Regarding the term *tanmātras*:
because there is nothing further beyond that, nothing else exists therein, the word *tanmātra* refers to sound and the other elements as being devoid of intermediate distinctions.]

Space provides room; wind is the life-sustainer; fire is the burner and the cooker; water is the nourisher and is liquid by nature; earth is the supporter. (As for "as," it means: just as in a banyan seed, by its own appropriate form...)
Just as sprouts, leaves, and fruits remain [within the seed], so too this entire universe— endowed with the manifold variety of bodies, organs, and other forms—
resides within the seed of the Heart, like the fluid within a peacock's egg.

Like the skill of an artisan in conceiving the variety of full lines, such as the primary and secondary feathers that have entered into every part of a peacock's tail, this must be discerned with subtle observation by those whose wealth is concentration. [The seed of the banyan tree exists there] in the form of a potentiality.
It is like a great tree; likewise, this entire universe of moving and non-moving beings resides within the seed-syllable of the heart.

According to the principle of the sacred tradition (*āmnāya*), this entire universe is contained within the Heart-seed-syllable (*hṛdayabīja*) in the form of the Supreme Goddess (*parābhaṭṭārikā*). How so?
Just as the ultimate reality (*pāramārthika-rūpa*) of transformations of clay, such as pots, bowls, and the like, [is clay itself].
Just as the established nature of substances such as water, when investigated, is found to be nothing other than the commonality of water and so forth, so too,
when the true essence of the principles (tattvas) beginning with earth and ending with Māyā is scrutinized, [it is found to be the same].

It becomes simply "sat. When this word is also analyzed, setting aside the suffixal portion which manifests the meaning of the verbal root, only the letter *sa*, consisting of the stem alone, remains; within that is the thirty-first principle (*tattva*), and beyond that—

The principles (tattvas) of Śuddhavidyeśvara and Sadāśiva, whose essence consists of knowledge and action, are included within the syllable *au*, which takes the form of acceptance (*abhyupagama*) and is composed of the unsurpassed power (*anuttara-śakti*), because they are specific manifestations of that power. Therefore:

The *visarjanīya* (the letter *ḥ*) consists of an emission directed both upward and downward; thus, for this seed-syllable of the heart which is of the nature of the Great Mantra (*mahāmantra*), it is composed of the universe (*viśvamaya*) and yet transcends the universe (*viśvottīrṇa*).
Herein, being of all forms (*sarvākāratva*) and being formless (*nirākāratva*) are respectively the causes.
Paramaśiva alone, transcending all, is one's own essential nature (*nijasvabhāva*), because He is the locus of both emergence and repose.

He who knows this seed of the Heart (*hṛdayabīja*) in its true essence and enters into it is, in the ultimate sense, truly initiated (*dīkṣita*). [Regarding the term "initiated": this true knowledge itself, devoid of offerings of sesame seeds and clarified butter, is initiation in its true essence.]

The sense is that [this is] initiation (*dīkṣā*). One who maintains the vital breaths while conducting oneself like an ordinary person becomes liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*); upon the fall of the body, one becomes none other than the venerable Lord Paramaśiva.
Thus ends the *Parāprāveśikā*, composed by the illustrious and eminent teacher of Mahāmāheśvara, Kṣemarāja.
When the assembly of texts and learned scholars— the refuge of the six sciences— had undergone decline due to the course of time,
[the author], being solely intent on the desire to uphold those various true dharmas...
For the performance of action by one endowed with the vigor of true discernment. || 1 ||
Having deliberated with his chief ministers who were devoted to righteousness, the illustrious sovereign of Kashmir established [this work],
which is filled with spiritual knowledge and worldly wisdom.
That which is the primary office for the extraction of texts. || 2 ||

May this [work], being refined through completion, purification, and exposition by virtuous persons who have entered upon the right livelihood and rely on Mukunda as their presiding authority, be auspicious.
This completed work is for the welfare of the virtuous. || 3 ||
(Mark) May this offering to the auspicious Śiva of one's own self be a bestower of auspiciousness for the student, the listener, and the investigator.
